text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point.
- Each token in the group account pays 0.3 points to every member of the group, you included, whoever put it there.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking: This is a public goods game where each token contributed returns only 0.3 to me but 0.9 to others, so keeping everything is the individually rational choice even though full cooperation maximizes the group total. With 10 repeated rounds, backward induction says defection is dominant throughout, but I'm weighing whether some contribution could help sustain cooperation anyway.

So individually it's dominant to keep everything, but collectively everyone contributing maximizes total payoff—the classic tension between selfish and cooperative strategies.

With 10 repeated rounds and finite horizon, backward induction suggests defection is the equilibrium, though I could consider cooperating early to build trust norms. Weighing this out, I'll go with contributing 0 as the simplest, rational choice given the math favors keeping tokens.
